claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity in high-temperature MPEAs are governed primarily by formation of a continuous, adherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer.
Protective oxide formation depends on the presence and distribution of oxygen-affine elements such as Al or Cr.
The ability of Al or Cr to diffuse to the surface affects protective oxide formation.
Alloy composition and microstructure control the availability and mobility of protective-scale-forming elements at elevated temperatures.
Systematically varying Al and Cr while maintaining comparable microstructures provides a controlled comparison of their effects.
The proposed structural mediator is a continuous Al2O3 or Cr2O3 surface scale.
The formation of a continuous Al2O3 or Cr2O3 scale depends on local Al or Cr concentration, distribution, and diffusion rate.
Al and Cr have high oxygen affinity and diffuse to the surface to form protective oxide scales.
Scale continuity and adherence limit further oxidation.
Limiting further oxidation preserves material integrity.
Insufficient concentration or mobility of Al or Cr causes non-protective oxide formation, rapid oxidation, and degradation.
MPEAs with sufficient Al or Cr will show lower oxidation mass gain than otherwise comparable alloys lacking these elements.
MPEAs with sufficient Al or Cr will form continuous protective oxide scales.
MPEAs with sufficient Al or Cr will undergo less mechanical-property degradation than alloys lacking Al or Cr.
The protective effect may reduce oxidation mass gain by approximately an order of magnitude relative to the baseline.
Low- or zero-Al/Cr baseline MPEAs are expected to show higher oxidation rates, non-protective oxides, and greater loss of material integrity.
The hypothesis is expected to apply above 900°C in oxidizing atmospheres when microstructure and grain size are comparable.
A threshold Al or Cr content is required for protective-scale formation.
Exposure in air at 1000°C for 100 hours, followed by mass-gain, scale, and mechanical-property measurements, can test the hypothesis.
Failure of Al/Cr-containing alloys to form continuous scales or outperform low-Al/Cr controls in oxidation and integrity would falsify the hypothesis.
